opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of the most interesting ideas come from the boundaries between fields, not from the middle of one field. ReAct is a good example. Before it, people working on language models were mostly thinking about reasoning: chain of thought, getting the model to think step by step to solve math or QA problems. Separately, people in reinforcement learning and robotics were thinking about agents acting in environments, taking actions and getting observations. These two communities used different benchmarks, read different papers, and had different intuitions about what intelligence is.

What ReAct did was quite simple: reasoning and acting shouldn't be separate. When humans solve a problem, we think a bit, do something, look at what happens, and think again. Reasoning helps you decide how to act, and acting gives you new information to reason about. That's obvious once you say it, but if you only live in the NLP world, you think of the model as something that takes text in and gives text out. And if you only live in the RL world, you think of the agent as a policy mapping observations to actions, and "thinking" isn't really an action. You need to stand somewhere in between to see that thinking can be a kind of action, one that doesn't change the external world but changes your internal state.

There's also something deeper. My background touches a bit of cognitive science and how humans use language, and I think language is special because it's the tool humans use to generalize. That perspective made it natural to see language not just as the task, but as the medium through which an agent reasons and plans.

So crossing boundaries matters because the problems we care about now, like building general agents, don't belong to any single discipline. If you only optimize within one field's benchmarks and assumptions, you make incremental progress. The bigger shifts usually come from noticing that two things people treated as separate are actually the same thing, or should be combined. And practically, a field's blind spots are often another field's common sense, so if you've been exposed to both, some ideas that look creative are really just you bringing over something that's obvious elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response says ReAct combined language-model reasoning associated with NLP and acting in environments associated with reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It explains that staying within NLP or RL limits what researchers notice, and that single-field benchmarks and assumptions can constrain progress toward general agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think ReAct is a pretty good example of why this matters, because the idea itself is almost embarrassingly simple once you say it out loud. People had been doing chain-of-thought prompting, where the model reasons step by step but can't touch the world. And in parallel, people were doing action-based things, like WebShop or ALFWorld, where an agent takes actions in an environment but doesn't really think. These two communities barely talked to each other. One was more NLP and language modeling, the other was more reinforcement learning and embodied agents. ReAct is just saying: why not interleave them? Reason, then act, then look at what came back, then reason again. That's it. The reason it hadn't been done wasn't that it was hard, it was that nobody was standing in both rooms at the same time.

So for me, crossing boundaries isn't some abstract virtue. It's where the low-hanging fruit is. When you stay inside one field, everyone is looking at the same problems with the same tools, and the remaining questions are genuinely hard because the easy ones got picked already. When you bring a tool from one field into another, suddenly things that looked hard become easy, or problems that nobody even noticed become visible.

I also think there's a deeper point about what intelligence actually is. Humans don't separate thinking from doing. You plan a little, you try something, it fails, you update, you try again. Language is how we think, and it's also how we interact with the world, asking questions, reading instructions, writing things down. If you only study language in isolation, you get a model that's very articulate but can't do anything. If you only study acting, you get something that's capable in a narrow environment but has no general knowledge or common sense. The interesting thing about language models is that for the first time, one system can potentially be both. But to even see that possibility, you need to have been exposed to both worlds.

My own background was kind of accidental in this sense. I came from a more traditional computer science and systems side, then got into NLP, and then spent a lot of time thinking about RL and agents during my PhD. Each time I switched, I felt like a beginner again, which is uncomfortable. But that discomfort is also where the ideas came from. A lot of my work, ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, WebShop, is basically me noticing that two things people treat as separate are actually the same thing from a slightly different angle.

So my advice to younger researchers is usually: don't be too loyal to your subfield. Read papers that aren't in your area, and go talk to the people who use different vocabulary than you do. Often they're solving your problem and don't know it, or you're solving theirs.

r001.rationale: The response says ReAct brings together chain-of-thought work from NLP and action-based work associated with reinforcement learning and agents, interleaving reasoning and acting.

r002.rationale: It says researchers who stay within one field face a narrower shared set of problems, while crossing fields can reveal new problems and make difficult ones easier to tackle.

astra-6.text:
I think crossing disciplinary boundaries helps us ask better questions. In AI, we often organize research around particular methods or tasks, but intelligence doesn’t necessarily respect those divisions. Reasoning, language, and interaction with an environment are closely connected.

ReAct is an example of taking that connection seriously. Instead of treating reasoning and acting as separate capabilities, we can let them support each other: reasoning helps decide what action to take, and the result of that action gives us new information that can change our reasoning. That creates a feedback loop.

For me, the value of crossing boundaries is finding those connections. It’s not just borrowing a technique from another field; it’s stepping back and asking whether a boundary we’ve inherited is preventing us from seeing a useful way to approach the problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses connecting reasoning and action, but does not attribute ReAct’s development to bridging natural language processing and reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It says inherited boundaries may hide useful approaches, but does not suggest that immersion in one disciplinary community makes general research harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I think disciplinary boundaries are useful for organizing knowledge, but the problems we want to solve don’t necessarily respect those boundaries. If you want to build an intelligent agent, you have to ask how reasoning, action, and feedback work together. That question connects language processing, reinforcement learning, and ideas about human cognition.

ReAct is a concrete example. A model can reason about what to do next, take an action—such as looking something up—and then use the observation to revise its reasoning. Reasoning helps guide action, and action provides information that reasoning alone may be missing.

When you look across fields, you can recognize that things usually studied separately might actually complement each other. For me, the point isn’t to cross boundaries for its own sake. It’s to start from the problem and bring together the ideas needed to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response connects language processing and reinforcement learning to intelligent-agent research and presents ReAct as an example, but it does not clearly attribute ReAct’s development to bridging those fields.

r002.rationale: The response says fields are often studied separately, but does not suggest that immersion in one disciplinary community makes pursuing more general research harder.
